items.abstract: <jats:p>Flexible building loads can reduce costs and relieve power networks, but fleet control must coordinate heterogeneous devices without creating demand peaks, comfort violations, or feeder overload. Large language model (LLM) agents promise adaptable, zero-shot control, but their operational value remains unclear because comparisons with trained numerical controllers rarely use matched trajectories or consistently account for uncertainty and inference cost. We address this gap with DRBENCH, a commonevaluation frameworkfor rule-based control, model predictive control (MPC), reinforcement learning (RL), coordinated and residual RL, and three LLM-agent designs. The framework couples building and device dynamics through a shared feeder, evaluates methods on identical episodes with paired statistics, measures inference overhead, and examines transfer to CityLearn data. The findingsshow that flexible language reasoning alone does not produce effective real-time dispatch. In the synthetic evaluation, PPO and SAC outperform all evaluated online LLM agents on cost and peak control and avoid the observed feeder overloads. Direct LLM control increases the weekly bill by $309 relative to PPO, while online LLM decisions are 1,000–10,000 times slower than learned-policy inference. Residual RL gives the strongest mean performance, indicating that learning benefits from refining a structured control prior. CityLearn provides an important qualification: direct and ReAct agents improve on a fixed time-of-use rule but not on MPC, and RL is not evaluated in that setting. Overall, the evidence supports numerical controllers for operational dispatch and positions LLMs more credibly as offline aids for specification, reward design, and controller configuration.</jats:p>
title: Benchmarking Large Language Model Agents against Reinforcement Learning for Building Demand Response

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper aims to examine where large language models (LLMs) and AI agents create the most value across the broader HR cycle – from workforce planning and attraction to offboarding – and where human oversight remains essential in higher-stakes decisions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper is a selective narrative review of recent academic literature on AI-enabled HRM, with emphasis on studies published between 2021 and 2025 that describe concrete applications of LLMs or agentic systems across employee-lifecycle stages and related HR functions. The review synthesises evidence for a practitioner audience and translates it into a decision framework for HR leaders.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three patterns stand out. Firstly, LLMs are most useful where HR work is knowledge intensive and language heavy, such as onboarding, learning support, employee self-service and document-rich compensation queries. Secondly, AI agents add value when HR work requires orchestration across multiple steps, tools or rules, particularly in recruitment workflows, guided onboarding and case handling. Thirdly, a full-cycle view shows uneven evidence: recruitment, onboarding and learning are the most developed domains, whereas workforce planning, engagement and retention and offboarding remain promising but less mature. Across all stages, the main barriers to responsible adoption are fairness, privacy, explainability, data quality and employee trust. High-stakes decisions such as selection, pay and performance evaluation therefore require human review, documented controls and clear appeal paths.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper moves beyond broad “AI in HR” claims by distinguishing between LLMs and AI agents, comparing their value across the HR cycle and offering practical guidance on where augmentation is more appropriate than automation. It also extends the discussion beyond the usual focus on recruitment and onboarding by mapping emerging use cases across the full employee lifecycle.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Beyond automation: where AI agents and large language models add value across the HR lifecycle

items.abstract: <jats:p>This study develops a structured benchmarking framework to evaluate hallucination phenomena across multimodal large language models (MLLMs), integrating text, image, and video modalities. Drawing from recent benchmark-driven studies and surveys, the research synthesizes taxonomies, detection strategies, and mitigation techniques to propose a unified evaluation protocol. Findings indicate that hallucination manifests differently across modalities, with video-based models exhibiting higher temporal inconsistency and image-language models showing relational fabrication under ambiguous prompts. The study concludes by proposing a harmonized, taxonomy-driven benchmark that integrates cognitive-inspired categorization and retrieval-based mitigation as core evaluation components.</jats:p>
title: <p>Benchmarking Hallucination Across Multimodal Large Language Models</p>

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Code-generating large language models have advanced rapidly from function-level synthesis to practical programming and repository-level software maintenance. Yet the scientific value of these advances depends critically on benchmark quality, evaluation rigour, and reproducibility. This paper presents a structured analytical review of the benchmark ecosystem for code-generating large language models and coding agents, with emphasis on execution-based evaluation, benchmark design quality, and cross-phase software-engineering coverage. The review synthesises foundational and recent primary sources spanning HumanEval, MBPP, APPS, MultiPL-E, DS-1000, BigCodeBench, SWE bench, and contemporary survey and benchmark-audit literature. Across these sources, the field has progressed from small Python-only tasks to multilingual, domain-specific, tool use, and repository-level benchmarks; however, current benchmark coverage remains imbalanced, with approximately 60% of surveyed benchmarks concentrated in the software-development phase and only small fractions devoted to requirements and design. Recent benchmark audits further show that nearly 70% of code-related benchmarks lacked explicit data-quality assurance measures, while many omitted key details required for reproducibility.&nbsp; 
<div>
 In response, this paper proposes a reproducibility-centred benchmark protocol for future evaluations. The protocol combines official benchmark releases, prompt canonicalisation, containerised execution, stronger execution oracles, contamination-aware reporting, and benchmark portfolios that span multiple software-development-life-cycle phases. The main conclusion is that benchmark design, not model scaling alone, has become the central bottleneck in credible research on automated code generation. Accordingly, the paper recommends a shift from single-benchmark reporting toward benchmark portfolios that jointly assess correctness, robustness, language breadth, practical tool use, and repository level maintenance. The resulting manuscript is intended to be directly adaptable for submission to a general computer-science venue.&nbsp;
</div></jats:p>
title: Computer Science: Reproducible Benchmarking of Code-Generating Large Language Models Across the Software Development Life Cycle
